summary: Gives guidance, based on operational experience, on choosing NSEC3 parameters for DNSSEC. NSEC3 proves that a name does not exist without exposing neighboring names directly. This Best Current Practice updates RFC 5155 with advice about selecting parameters.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC proves that a domain name does not exist by publishing signed records. NSEC3 does this with hashed names, so that the list of real names in a zone is not published in clear text. This Best Current Practice says how to set the four NSEC3 options: use SHA-1, run no extra hash rounds, use no salt, and keep the opt-out flag off unless the zone is very large and mostly unsigned.

subtitle: How to set the NSEC3 hash algorithm, iteration count, salt and opt-out flag in a DNSSEC-signed zone.

tldr.problem: NSEC3 proves that a name does not exist by publishing hashed names, and its settings decide how much work a server does and how hard the zone is to enumerate. Zone owners had no published advice on good values to choose.
tldr.mechanism: The document recommends the NSEC3PARAM settings of SHA-1, 0 extra iterations and an empty salt for every zone, says that NSEC should be preferred where NSEC3 is not needed, and tells validating resolvers to lower the iteration counts they accept.
tldr.outcome: It updates the guidance in RFC 5155 with a single recommended configuration, and it introduces Extended DNS Error code 27 so a resolver can say that it refused an unsupported iteration count.

facts.label: Hash algorithm in use on the Internet

today: RFC 9276 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 236, published in August 2022. It updates RFC 5155 with guidance on choosing NSEC3 iteration and salt parameters, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What NSEC3 Does and Why the Settings Matter
sections.content:
NSEC3 gives a DNSSEC-signed zone a way to prove that a name or a record type does not exist, using signed DNS records. Unlike its counterpart NSEC, NSEC3 does not publish the bounding domain name pairs directly. Instead the names of valid nodes in the zone are obfuscated by hashing them, possibly more than once. The RFC notes that currently only SHA-1 is in use on the Internet for this.

NSEC3 also offers opt-out support, which lets a block of unsigned delegations be covered by a single NSEC3 record. With opt-out, a large registry only has to sign as many NSEC3 records as there are signed DS or other resource record sets in the zone. The document states plainly that this sacrifices the tamper resistance of the proof of nonexistence in order to reduce memory and CPU overheads.

The tunable parameters live in an NSEC3PARAM record at the zone apex. There are four of them: the hash algorithm, the processing flags, the number of hash iterations and the salt. Each has security and operational effects for both zone owners and validating resolvers, and this document gives best-practice recommendations for setting them. It updates RFC 5155 with guidance about selecting the iteration and salt parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: NSEC3 lets a DNS zone prove that a name is missing without printing the zone's real names. It does this by hashing each name before signing it. The zone's owner sets four options for this hashing, and this document says which values to use.

sections.title: Flags and the Opt-Out Shortcut
sections.content:
The algorithm field is not discussed by this document; readers are pointed to RFC 8624 for guidance about DNSSEC algorithm usage.

The NSEC3PARAM flags field currently contains only reserved and unassigned flags. Individual NSEC3 records, however, carry an Opt-Out flag that specifies whether that record provides proof of nonexistence.

In general, NSEC3 with the Opt-Out flag enabled should only be used in large, highly dynamic zones with a small percentage of signed delegations. Operationally this allows for fewer signature creations when new delegations are inserted into a zone. The document says this is typically only necessary for extremely large registration points that provide zone updates faster than real-time signing allows, or that run on memory-constrained hardware. Operators considering the use of NSEC3 are advised to weigh the costs and benefits of choosing NSEC3 over NSEC carefully. Smaller zones, or large but relatively static zones, are encouraged not to use the opt-out flag and to take advantage of DNSSEC's authenticated denial of existence instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The opt-out flag lets one signed record stand in for many unsigned delegations, which saves signing work but weakens the proof. The document says to use it only for very large zones that change quickly, and to leave it off everywhere else.

sections.title: Iterations and What the Count Means
sections.content:
NSEC3 records are created by first hashing the input domain and then repeating that hashing with the same algorithm a number of times, based on the iteration parameter in the NSEC3PARAM and NSEC3 records. The first hash with NSEC3 is typically sufficient to discourage zone enumeration performed by walking an unhashed NSEC chain.

The count needs care. RFC 5155 describes the Iterations field as the number of additional times the hash function has been performed, so an NSEC3 record with an Iterations field of 0 actually requires one hash iteration.

The document's reasoning is that only determined parties with significant resources are likely to try to uncover hashed values, regardless of the number of additional iterations performed. An adversary who wants to spend CPU on an offline dictionary attack will likely find most of the guessable names despite any level of additional iterations. Most names published in the DNS are rarely secret or unpredictable: they are published to be memorable, used and consumed by humans, and they are often recorded in many other network logs such as email logs, certificate transparency logs, web page links, intrusion-detection systems, malware scanners and email archives. Many times a simple dictionary of commonly used domain name prefixes, such as www, mail, imap, login and database, can quickly reveal a large number of labels within a zone. Because of this, there are increasing performance costs and diminishing returns associated with applying additional hash iterations beyond the first.

Although Section 10.3 of RFC 5155 specifies upper bounds for the number of hash iterations to use, there was no published guidance for zone owners about good values to select. Recent academic studies have shown that NSEC3 hashing provides only moderate protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The iteration count is the number of extra times a name is hashed on top of the first hash, so a count of 0 still means one hash. Extra rounds cost server time and rarely stop an attacker who is willing to spend it, because real names are easy to guess and are recorded in many other logs.

sections.title: Salt and the Cost of Changing It
sections.content:
NSEC3 records provide an additional salt value, which can be combined with a fully qualified domain name to influence the resulting hash, but the properties of this extra salt are complicated.

In cryptography, salts generally add a layer of protection against offline, stored dictionary attacks by combining the value to be hashed with a unique salt value. This prevents adversaries from building up and remembering a single dictionary of values that can translate a hash output back to the value it was derived from. In the case of DNS the situation is different, because the hashed names placed in NSEC3 records are always implicitly salted by hashing the fully qualified domain name from each zone. Thus no single pre-computed table works to speed up dictionary attacks against multiple target zones, and an attacker is always required to compute a complete dictionary per zone, which is expensive in both storage and CPU time.

A typical zone walking attack has two phases. In the online phase, the attacker walks the zone by enumerating almost all the hashes listed in NSEC3 records and storing them for the offline phase. In the offline cracking phase, the attacker attempts to crack the underlying hash. The additional salt value raises the cost of the attack only if the salt value changes during the online phase of the attack. In other words, an additional, constant salt value does not change the cost of the attack.

Changing a zone's salt value requires the construction of a complete new NSEC3 chain. This is true both when re-signing the entire zone at once and when incrementally signing it in the background, where the new salt is only activated once every name in the chain has been completed. Re-salting is therefore a very complex operation, with significant CPU time, memory and bandwidth consumption, which makes very frequent re-salting impractical and renders the additional salt field functionally useless.
sections.plainLanguage: The salt is an extra value mixed into the hash. It only slows an attacker down if it changes while the attacker is collecting hashes, and changing it means building and signing a whole new set of records. A salt that never changes therefore buys nothing.

sections.title: Advice for Zone Publishers
sections.content:
First, if the operational or security features of NSEC3 are not needed, then NSEC SHOULD be used in preference to NSEC3. NSEC3 requires greater computational power for both authoritative servers and validating clients. There is a nontrivial complexity in finding matching NSEC3 records to randomly generated prefixes within a DNS zone, and NSEC mitigates this concern. If NSEC3 must be used, then an iterations count of 0 MUST be used to alleviate computational burdens. Extra iteration counts other than 0 increase the impact of CPU-exhausting DoS attacks, and also increase the risk of interoperability problems.

Deploying NSEC with minimally covering NSEC records, as described in RFC 4470, also incurs a cost, and zone owners should measure the computational difference in deploying either RFC 4470 or NSEC3.

For all zones, the recommended NSEC3 parameters are shown below, with SHA-1, no extra iterations and an empty salt:

bcp.example. IN NSEC3PARAM 1 0 0 -

For small zones, the use of opt-out-based NSEC3 records is NOT RECOMMENDED. For very large and sparsely signed zones, where the majority of the records are insecure delegations, opt-out MAY be used. Operators SHOULD NOT use a salt, indicating a zero-length salt value instead, which is written as a hyphen in the presentation format.

If salts are used, note that since the NSEC3PARAM RR is not used by validating resolvers, the iterations and salt parameters can be changed without the need to wait for resource record sets to expire from caches. A complete new NSEC3 chain needs to be constructed and the full zone needs to be re-signed.
sections.plainLanguage: Use plain NSEC unless you need something NSEC3 alone provides. If you do use NSEC3, set the iteration count to 0 and leave the salt empty, and only turn on opt-out for very large zones where most records are unsigned.

sections.title: Advice for Validating Resolvers
sections.content:
Because there has been a large growth of open, public DNSSEC validating resolvers that are subject to compute resource constraints when handling requests from anonymous clients, this document recommends that validating resolvers reduce their iteration count limits over time. Validating resolver operators and software implementers are encouraged to continue evaluating NSEC3 iteration count deployment trends and lower their acceptable iteration limits over time. Because treating a high iteration count as insecure leaves zones subject to attack, they are further encouraged to lower their default limit for returning SERVFAIL when processing NSEC3 parameters containing large iteration count values.

Validating resolvers MAY return an insecure response to their clients when processing NSEC3 records with iterations larger than 0. A validating resolver returning an insecure response MUST still validate the signature over the NSEC3 record, to ensure the iteration count was not altered since record publication. Validating resolvers MAY also return a SERVFAIL response, and MAY choose to ignore authoritative server responses with iteration counts greater than 0, which will likely result in a SERVFAIL to the client when no acceptable responses are received from authoritative servers.

A validating resolver returning an insecure or SERVFAIL answer to its client, after receiving and validating an unsupported NSEC3 parameter from the authoritative server, SHOULD return an Extended DNS Error (EDE) EDNS0 option of value 27. A validating resolver that chooses to ignore a response with an unsupported iteration count, and that does not validate the signature, MUST NOT return this EDE option.

The document notes that this specification updates RFC 5155 by significantly decreasing the requirements originally specified in Section 10.3 of that RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver that checks signatures may refuse to handle a zone whose records were hashed too many times. It can either answer without a security flag or report a failure, and it should tell the client which one it did using error code 27. It must still check the signature before answering in that way.

sections.title: Advice for Primary and Secondary Servers
sections.content:
Primary and secondary authoritative servers for a zone that are not being run by the same operational staff, or not using the same software and configuration, must take into account the potential differences in NSEC3 iteration support.

Operators of secondary services should advertise the parameter limits that their servers support. Correspondingly, operators of primary servers need to ensure that their secondaries support the NSEC3 parameters they expect to use in their zones. To ensure reliability, after primaries change their iteration counts, they should query their secondaries with known nonexistent labels to verify that the secondary servers are responding as expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Two servers that copy the same zone can still disagree about how many hash rounds they accept. Each one should say what it supports, and the server that publishes the zone should check the copy by asking it for a name that does not exist.

sections.title: Security and Operational Cost
sections.content:
The document states that the whole of it discusses security and operational considerations with various parameter selections of NSEC3 and NSEC3PARAM fields.

The point where a validating resolver returns an insecure response, compared with the point where it returns SERVFAIL, must be considered carefully. When a validating resolver treats a zone as insecure above a particular value, say 100, and returns SERVFAIL above a higher point, say 500, it leaves the zone subject to attacker-in-the-middle attacks as if it were unsigned between these values. Validating resolver operators and software implementers SHOULD set the point above which a zone is treated as insecure to the same as the point where the resolver begins returning SERVFAIL.

Appendix A reports the measurements taken at the time of publication: an upper limit of 100 iterations for treating a zone as insecure was interoperable without significant problems, but at the same time still enabled CPU-exhausting DoS attacks, and returning SERVFAIL beyond 500 iterations appeared to be interoperable without significant problems.

Appendix B gives the cost. The queries per second of authoritative servers decrease because of the computational overhead of processing DNS requests for zones with higher NSEC3 iteration counts: 89 percent of the zero-iteration rate at 10 iterations, 82 percent at 20, 64 percent at 50, 47 percent at 100 and 38 percent at 150.
sections.plainLanguage: Two limits have to match: the point where a resolver stops trusting a zone and the point where it reports failure. If they differ, a zone looks unsigned in between. More hash rounds also cut the number of queries a server can answer each second, so the cost is easy to measure.

items.title: Hash algorithm
items.text: Which hash function is applied to each name. SHA-1 is the one in use on the Internet.

items.title: Processing flags
items.text: Currently only reserved and unassigned flags are used.

items.title: Hash iterations
items.text: The number of extra times the hash is applied on top of the first hash.

items.title: Salt
items.text: An extra value mixed into the hash, given as a zero-length value to disable it.
